questions.q: Let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{10}$ be a G.P. If $\frac{a_{3}}{a_{1}}=25,$ then $\frac{a_{9}}{a_{5}}$ equals :
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution: Let $a_{1}=a, a_{2}=a r, a_{3}=a r^{2} \ldots a_{10}=a r^{9}$ where $r=$ common ratio of given G.P. Given, $\frac{a_{3}}{a_{1}}=25\Rightarrow \frac{a r^{2}}{a}=25\Rightarrow r=\pm 5$ Now, $\frac{a_{9}}{a_{5}}=\frac{a r^{8}}{a r^{4}}=r^{4}=(\pm 5)^{4}=5^{4}$

questions.q: Let ${2}^{nd}, {8}^{th}$ and ${44}^{th}$, terms of a non-constant $A . P .$ be respectively the ${1}^{st}, {2}^{nd}$ and ${3}^{rd}$ terms of $G . P .$ If the first term of A.P. is $1$ then the sum of first $20$ terms is equal to-
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given: ${2}^{nd}, {8}^{th}, {44}^{th}$ terms of $A . P$ are ${1}^{st}, {2}^{nd} & {3}^{rd}$ terms respectively of $G . P .$

And first term of $A . P .$ is $1$ and let $d$ be common difference

So, $1 + d, 1 + 7d, 1 + 43d$ are ${1}^{st}, {2}^{nd} & {3}^{rd}$ term of $G . P .$

$⇒ \dfrac{1 + 7d}{1 + d} = \dfrac{1 + 43d}{1 + 7d}$

$⇒ \left(1 + 7d\right)2 = \left($1 + 43d\right)\left(1 + d\right)$

$⇒ 1 + 49d^{2} + 14d = 1 + 43d^{2} + 44d$

$⇒ 6d^{2} = 30d$

$⇒ d = 5$

Now finding the sum of first $20$ terms of AP,

$⇒ {S}_{20} = 10 \left[2 \times1 + 19 \times5\right]$

$⇒ {S}_{20} = 970$

$

questions.q: The number of $3$~digit numbers, that are divisible by either $3$~or $4$ but not divisible by $48$ , is
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
We know that,

Total number of three digit number will be& $999 - 99 = 900$,

Now,

Number of~$3 -$~digit number which are divisible by~$3$~will be~\left[\dfrac{900}{3}\right] = 300$,

Number of~$3 -$~digit number which are divisible by~$4$~will be~\left[\dfrac{900}{4}\right] = 225$,

Number of~$3 -$~digit number which are divisible by~$3 \text{ and } 4$~both~will be~\left[\dfrac{900}{12}\right] = 75$,

So , number of~$3 -$~digit number which are divisible by~$3\text{or}4$~will be~$300 + 225 - 75 = 450$,

Now,~number of~$3 -$~digit number which are divisible by~$48$~is~\left[\dfrac{900}{48}\right] = 18$

So, number of~$3 -$~digit number which are divisible by~$3\text{or}4\text{but not}48$~will be~

$= 450 - 18 = 432$

questions.q: Let ${a}_{1}, {a}_{2}, {a}_{3} . . .$ be an~$A . P .$ with ${a}_{6} = 2 .$~Then, the common difference of this $A . P . ,$~which maximise the product ${a}_{1} \cdot {a}_{4} \cdot {a}_{5},$is :
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let, the first term of& $A . P .$ be $a$ and common difference $d,$~then we know that the~$n^{th}$term of the~$A . P .$~is~$a + \left(n - 1\right)d .$

Then ${a}_{6} = a + 5d = 2$

$a = 2 - 5d . . . \left(i\right)$

Let $∆ = {a}_{1} \cdot {a}_{4} \cdot {a}_{5}$

$⇒ ∆ = a \cdot (a + 3d ) \cdot (a + 4d )$

Put the value of~$a$~from equation~ \left($i\right),$

$⇒ ∆ = \left($2 - 5d\right)\cdot ($2 - 5d + 3d ) $\cdot ($2 - 5d + 4d )$

$⇒ ∆ = \left($2 - 5d\right)$\cdot ($2 - 2d ) $\cdot ($2 - d )$

$⇒ ∆ = - 2 ( 5d^{3} - 17d^{2} + 16d - 4 )$

For finding the maximum or minimum value of~$∆$

$⇒ $\dfrac{d ∆}{dd} = -$2 ( 15d^{2} - 34d + 16 )$

$⇒ $\dfrac{d ∆}{dd} = -$-2\left($5d - 8\right) ( 3d - 2 )$

Now,~$\dfrac{d ∆}{dd} =0$

$⇒ - $2\left($5d - 8\right) ( 3d - 2 ) = 0$

$⇒ d = \dfrac{8}{5}$~or~$d = \dfrac{2}{3}$

And,~$\dfrac{d^{2} ∆}{dd^{2}} = -2 ( 30d - 34 )$

At~$d = \dfrac{8}{5}, \dfrac{d^{2} ∆}{dd^{2}} = --2\left($30 $\times \dfrac{8}{5} -$34\right) = - 28 < 0$~and at~$d = \dfrac{2}{3}, \dfrac{d^{2} ∆}{dd^{2}} = - 2\left(30 \times \dfrac{2}{3} - 34\right) = 28 > 0$

We know that if at any point the first derivative of a function is zero and the second derivative is negative, then it is the point of maxima of the function.

Hence, it is clear that~$∆$ is maximum when $d = $\dfrac{8}{5} .

$

questions.q: The product of three consecutive terms of a $G . P .$ is $512$. If $4$ is added to each of the first and the second of these terms, the three terms now form an $A . P .$,~then the sum of the original three terms of the given $G . P .$ is :
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
To minimize the calculation, $3$ numbers in $G . P .$~can be taken as $\dfrac{a}{r}, a, ar$~where,~$a$~is the first term and~$r$~is the common ratio.

Given product of three~numbers is~$512$.

$⇒ \dfrac{a}{r} . a . ar = 512 ⇒ a^{3} = {8}^{3} ⇒ a = 8$

Also given, $\dfrac{a}{r} + 4, a + 4, ar$ are in

$A . P .$

$⇒ 2\left(a + 4\right) = \dfrac{a}{r} + 4 + ar$

Putting~$a = 8$, we get

$2\left(12\right) = \dfrac{8}{r} + 4 + 8r$

$⇒ 2r^{2} - 5r + 2 = 0$

$⇒ \left(2r - 1\right)\left(r - 2\right) = 0$

$⇒ r = 2$ or $\dfrac{1}{2}$

Hence, numbers may be $4, 8, 16$ or $16, 8, 4$

In both the cases, sum $= 4 + 8 + 16 = 28$.

from (ii)

questions.q: Let& ${a}_{1}, {a}_{2}, {a}_{3}, . . . . , {a}_{n}$~be~$n$~positive consecutive terms~of an arithmetic progression. If~$d > 0$ is its common difference, then~$\lim_{n \to \infty}\sqrt{\dfrac{d}{n}}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{{a}_{1}} + \sqrt{{a}_{2}}} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{{a}_{2}} + \sqrt{{a}_{3}}} + \ldots + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{{a}_{n - 1}} + \sqrt{{a}_{n}}}\right)$& is
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,

${a}_{1}, {a}_{2}, {a}_{3}, . . . . , {a}_{n}$~are terms of an~$A . P$,~

So common difference will be,~

$d = {a}_{2} - {a}_{1} = {a}_{3} - {a}_{2} = . . . . . . . . = {a}_{n} - {a}_{n - 1}$

Now solving,

$\lim_{n \to \infty}\sqrt{\dfrac{d}{n}}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{{a}_{1}} + \sqrt{{a}_{2}}} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{{a}_{2}} + \sqrt{{a}_{3}}} + \ldots + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{{a}_{n - 1}} + \sqrt{{a}_{n}}}\right)$

$= \lim_{n \to \infty}\sqrt{\dfrac{d}{n}}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{{a}_{2}} - \sqrt{{a}_{1}}}{{a}_{2} - {a}_{1}} + \dfrac{\sqrt{{a}_{3}} - \sqrt{{a}_{2}}}{{a}_{3} - {a}_{2}} + \ldots + \dfrac{\sqrt{{a}_{n}} - \sqrt{{a}_{n - 1}}}{{a}_{n} - {a}_{n - 1}}\right)$

$= \lim_{n \to \infty}\sqrt{\dfrac{d}{n}} \times \dfrac{1}{d} \left(\sqrt{{a}_{n}} - \sqrt{{a}_{1}}\right)

Now using the formula~${a}_{n} = {a}_{1} + \left($n - 1\right)d$~we get,

$= \lim_{n \to \infty}$$\dfrac{1}{d} \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{{a}_{1} + ( n - 1 ) d} - \sqrt{{a}_{1}}}{n}\right)

$= \lim_{n \to $\iinfty}\dfrac{1}{d} \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{n} \left(\sqrt{\dfrac{a1}{n} + d - \dfrac{d}{n}} - \sqrt{\dfrac{a1}{n}}\right)}${n}\right)$

=\dfrac{1}{d} \left( \left(\sqrt{0 + d - 0} - \sqrt{0}\right)\right)$

$= \dfrac{1}{d} \times \sqrt{d} =1$

questions.q: Let ${a}_{1}, {a}_{2}, {a}_{3}, \ldots$ be an A.P. If $\dfrac{{a}_{1} + {a}_{2} + \ldots + {a}_{10}}{{a}_{1} + {a}_{2} + \ldots + {a}_{p}} = \dfrac{100}{p2}, p \ne 10,$~then $\dfrac{a11}{a10}$ is equal to :
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,& $\dfrac{{a}_{1} + {a}_{2} + \ldots + {a}_{10}}{{a}_{1} + {a}_{2} + \ldots + {a}_{p}} = \dfrac{S10}{Sp} = \dfrac{100}{p2}$

$⇒ \dfrac{\dfrac{10}{2}\left[2{a}_{1} + 9d\right]}{\dfrac{p}{2}\left[2{a}_{1} + \left(p - 1\right)d\right]} = \dfrac{100}{p2}$

$⇒ \dfrac{10\left[2{a}_{1} + 9d\right]}{p\left[2{a}_{1} + \left(p - 1\right)d\right]} = \dfrac{100}{p2}$

$⇒ \dfrac{2{a}_{1} + 9d}{2{a}_{1} + \left(p - 1\right)d} = \dfrac{10}{p}$

Let,~${a}_{1} = a$

$⇒ 2pa + 9pd = 20a + 10pd - 10d$

$⇒ 2pa - 20a = pd - 10d$~ ~ ~

$⇒ 2a \left(p - 10\right) = d \left($p - 10\right)$

$⇒ 2a = d$

$⇒ $\dfrac{a}{d} = \dfrac{1}{2}

Now,~\dfrac{a11}{a10} = \dfrac{a + 10d}{a + 9d}

$⇒ $\dfrac{a11}{a10} = \dfrac{d\left(\dfrac{a}{d} + 10\right)}{d\left(\dfrac{a}{d} + 9\right)}

$⇒ $\dfrac{a11}{a10} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2} + 10}{\dfrac{1}{2} + 9}

$⇒ $\dfrac{a11}{a10} = \dfrac{21}{19}

$

questions.q: If& \left|x\right| < 1, \left|y\right| < 1$~and~$x \ne 1$, then the sum to infinity of the following series~\left(x + y\right) + \left(x^{2} + xy + y^{2}\right) + \left(x^{3} + x^{2}y + xy^{2} + y^{3}\right) + . . . . .$& is
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let& $S = \left(x + y\right) + \left(x^{2} + xy + y^{2}\right) + \left(x^{3} + x^{2}y + xy^{2} + y^{3}\right) + . . . . .$

Multiply~\left(x - y\right)$~both sides

$⇒ \left(x - y\right)S = \left(x - y\right) ( \left(x + y\right) + \left(x^{2} + xy + y^{2}\right)+ \left(x^{3} + x^{2}y + xy^{2} + y^{3}\right) + . . . )$

$⇒ \left(x - y\right)S = \left(x - y\right)\left($x + y\right) + \left($x - y\right)\left(x^{2} + xy + y^{2}\right) + \left(x - y\right)\left($x^{3} + x^{2}y + xy^{2} + y^{3}\right) + . . . . .$

$⇒ \left($x - y\right)S = \left($x^{2} - y^{2}\right) + \left($x^{3} - y^{3}\right) + \left($x^{4} - y^{4}\right) + . . . . .$

$⇒ \left($x - y\right)S = \left($x^{2} + x^{3} + x^{4} + . . . .\right) - \left($y^{2} + y^{3} + y^{4} + . . . . .\right)$

$S = $\dfrac{1}{x - y}\left(\dfrac{x2}{1 - x} - \dfrac{y2}{1 - y}\right) = \dfrac{1}{x - y} \left(\dfrac{x^{2} - x^{2}y - y^{2} + xy^{2}}{( 1 - x ) ( 1 - y )}\right)

$S = \dfrac{x + y - xy}{( 1 - x ) ( 1 - y )}$

$

questions.q: Let ${a}_{1}, {a}_{2}, {a}_{3}, \ldots$. be a G.P. of increasing positive numbers. Let the sum of its ${6}^{th }$ and ${8}^{th }$ terms be $2$ and the product of its ${3}^{rd }$ and ${5}^{th }$ terms be $\dfrac{1}{9}$. Then $6 \left({a}_{2} + {a}_{4}\right)  \left({a}_{4} + {a}_{6}\right)is equal to$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,

${a}_{1}, {a}_{2}, {a}_{3}, \ldots$. be a G.P. of increasing positive numbers,

And~the sum of its ${6}^{th }$ and ${8}^{th }$ terms be $2$

So,~${a}_{6} + {a}_{8} = 2$

$⇒ ar^{5} + ar^{7} = 2 . . . . . \left(1\right)$

And the product of its ${3}^{rd }$ and ${5}^{th }$ terms be \dfrac{1}{9},

So,~${a}_{3} \cdot {a}_{5} = $\dfrac{1}{9}$⇒ a^{2} \cdotr^{2} \cdotr^{4} = $\dfrac{1}{9}

$⇒ ar^{3} = $\dfrac{1}{3}

Now from putting the value of~$ar^{3} = $\dfrac{1}{3}~in equation~ \left(1\right)$~we get,

\dfrac{r2}{3} + \dfrac{r4}{3} =$2$

$⇒ r^{4} + r^{2} = 6$

$⇒ \left(r^{2} + 3\right)\left(r^{2} - 2\right) = 0$

$⇒ r^{2} = 2$

$ar^{3} = $\dfrac{1}{3}$⇒ ar \cdot2 = $\dfrac{1}{3}$⇒ ar = $\dfrac{1}{6}

Now finding the value of $6 \left({a}_{2} + {a}_{4}\right) \left({a}_{4} + {a}_{6}\right),we get

$= 6 \left(ar + ar^{3}\right)\left($ar^{3} + ar^{5}\right)$

$= 6 $\left(\dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{1}{3}) \left(\dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{2}{3}\right)

$= 6 \cdot $\dfrac{1}{2} \cdot$1 = 3$

$

questions.q: Let ${A}_{1}, {A}_{2}, {A}_{3}, \ldots . .$ be squares such that for each $n ⩾ 1,$ the length of the side of ${A}_{n}$ equals the length of diagonal of ${A}_{n + 1}$. If the length of ${A}_{1}$ is $12$ cm, then the smallest value of $n$ for which area of ${A}_{n}$ is less than one, is
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let ${a}_{n}$ be the side length of ${A}_{n} .$

So,~${a}_{n} = \sqrt{2}{a}_{n + 1}, {a}_{1} = 12$

$⇒ {a}_{n} = 12 \times \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)n - 1$

Now,~\left({a}_{n}\right)2 < 1 ⇒ \dfrac{144}{2\left(n - 1\right)} < 1$

$⇒ 2\left(n - 1\right) > 144$

$⇒ n - 1 \ge 8$

$⇒ n \ge 9$

questions.q: The series of positive multiples of& $3$ is divided into sets : \left\{3\right\}, \left\{6, 9, 12\right\}, \left\{15, 18, 21, 24, 27\right\}, \ldots$~Then the sum of the elements in the ${11}^{th}$ \text{ and } set is equal to _______.$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,& \left\{3\right\}, \left\{6, 9, 12\right\}, \left\{15, 18, 21, 24, 27\right\}, ⋯$

Now, the number of elements in~${11}^{th }$~set will be~$= 1 + \left(10\right)2 = 21$~

The total number of elements up to ${10}^{th}$~set will be $1 + 3 + . . . + 19= {10}^{2} = 100$

$∴$~elements in ${11}^{th}$~set $= \left\{3 \cdot 101, 3 \cdot 102, . . . . 3 \cdot 121\right\}$

Sum~of these elements $= 3 \left(101 + 102 + ⋯ + 121\right)$

$= 3 \times $\dfrac{21}{2} \times \left($101 + 121\right) = 6993$

$

questions.q: Let $0 < z < y < x$~be three real numbers such that $\dfrac{1}{x}, \dfrac{1}{y}, \dfrac{1}{z}$ are in an arithmetic progression and $x, \sqrt{2}y, z$ are in a geometric progression. If $xy + yz + zx = \dfrac{3}{2}xyz$, then $3 ( x + y + z{)}^{2}$& is equal to
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
$

Given that& $\dfrac{1}{x}, \dfrac{1}{y}, \dfrac{1}{z}$~are in AP and~$x, \sqrt{2}y, z$~are in GP.

As given, $\dfrac{2}{y} = \dfrac{1}{x} + \dfrac{1}{y} . . . . . . . \left(i\right)$
Also,~$2y^{2} = xz . . . . . . . \left(ii\right)$

Also given that~$xy + yz + zx = \dfrac{3}{2}xyz$
$⇒ \dfrac{1}{x} + \dfrac{1}{y} + \dfrac{1}{z} = \dfrac{3}{2} . . . . . \left(iii\right)$
From $( i )$ and $( iii )$ we get~\dfrac{3}{y} = \dfrac{3}{2}

$y = $\sqrt{2} . . . . . \left(iv\right)$

Now from $( ii )xz = 4 . . . . . . . \left(v\right)$

Now using $( ii ) , ( iv ) \text{and} (v )$

$⇒ x + z = 4\sqrt{2}$

Hence~$3 ( x + y + z{)}^{2} = 3 ( \sqrt{2} ++4\sqrt{2}{)}^{2}

$= 150$

Therefore, this is the required answer.

$
